newsitem.title: INDONESIA: FOCUS-Jakarta stocks rebound undermined by rates.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Jakarta stocks rebound undermined by rates.

text.p: Jakarta stocks went on a wild rollercoaster ride on Tuesday after the central bank moved to quash speculation in the rupiah by raising interest rates, brokers said.
The Jakarta composite index fell in early trading, recovered some ground later on but plunged again at the close.

"The index had risen more than two percent on bargain-hunting in the morning. But the hike of rates in central bank certificates (SBIs) dashed hopes for even a slight rebound," said one broker with a large foreign brokerage.
The index closed down 9.11 points or 1.52 percent at 590.53. It swung between a high of 612.21 points and a low of 581.58 on fluctuating sentiment driven by the volatile rupiah currency.
In the end, the rate hike prevailed.
"The rise in the interest rates has helped the currency but it hasn't done much for the stock market," said Tom Inglis, head of research for ING Barings in Jakarta.
"Uncertainties in the currency and the interest rates will keep equities nervous."

Bank Indonesia, the central bank, announced that rates for one-week bilateral SBIs were being raised to 20 percent from 10.5 percent, two-week to 22 percent from 11 percent, one-month to 30 percent from 11.625 and three-months to 28 percent from 11.5 percent.
Analysts said the move was aimed at containing speculative attacks against the rupiah, which has fallen about 25 percent since the beginning of July.
"The rate hikes are quite high, indicating the current tight liquidity is expected to continue at least for the next three to four months," said Wilianto Ie, an analyst with Nava SC Securities.
The hikes prompted renewed heavy selling in stocks, particularly in the banking sector, which staged a brief rebound in morning trade on support from government institutions, brokers said.

Banking stocks were the hardest hit following the central bank's move, with blue-chips Bank Negara Indonesia and Bank Internasional Indonesia among the losers on expectations that funds will be more expensive, brokers said.
Bank Internasional Indonesia, one of the country's most profitable privately-owned banks, closed 50 rupiah lower at 1,225 rupiah. It had risen 75 rupiah before the rate hikes.
State-controlled Bank Negara Indonesia, Indonesia's largest bank, closed 75 rupiah lower at 1,175 rupiah. It had risen 25 rupiah earlier.

"Players had expected the index to rebound slightly as many stocks had been oversold. The rate hikes, however, have forced them to step back and think a thousand times before making a decision to buy," one broker said.

Jakarta stocks have been extremely weak this month, falling more than 130 points, or more than 18 percent, since August 1. They have tracked the weakness in the rupiah, which plunged to a historic low of 3,045 against the dollar on Tuesday.
The currency however rebounded after the rate hike and was last trading at 2,870/900.
The broker said some property stocks also staged a modest rebound in early trading, but closed lower due to the rate hikes.
Ciputra Development, one of Indonesia's largest property firms, was up 125 rupiah in early trading, but closed 100 rupiah lower at 1,200 rupiah.
Other property stocks that failed to sustain their early gains included Duta Pertiwi and Summarecon.
